clue.text: A nickel for a David Mamet play

explanation.surface: A coin is swapped for a playwright's script.
explanation.definitionFit: The buffalo nickel was a US five-cent coin bearing a bison, and Mamet wrote a 1975 play of that title about small-time crooks planning to steal a coin.

clue.text: Some of Richler's more agile characters

definitions.text: Some of Richler's more agile characters

parts.words: Some of Richler's more agile characters
parts.note: Mordecai Richler's first novel is titled after nimble circus performers, so its title figures are literally agile characters

explanation.surface: A remark about the nimblest people in Mordecai Richler's fiction.
explanation.definitionFit: Circus tumblers are agile performers, and Richler's 1954 debut novel bears their name as its title.

clue.text: Wellsian millionaire and bankrupt

parts.note: points to the patent-medicine tycoon in H. G. Wells's Tono-Bungay, who makes a vast fortune and then loses it

explanation.surface: A thumbnail of a rise-and-fall figure from H. G. Wells.
explanation.definitionFit: In Tono-Bungay the narrator's uncle grows rich selling a quack tonic, then collapses into ruin and flight.

clue.text: The whole earth is at rest, and is quiet: they break forth into singing." ()

definitions.text: The whole earth is at rest, and is quiet: they break forth into singing."

parts.words: The whole earth is at rest, and is quiet: they break forth into singing."
parts.note: the empty brackets ask for the source of this quotation, a verse from the Old Testament prophet's book (chapter 14, verse 7)

explanation.surface: A Bible verse quoted with its reference left blank for the solver.
explanation.definitionFit: The verse comes from the fourteenth chapter of the prophetic book in the Old Testament, so the book's name fills the citation.

clue.text: Personal assistant gives offbeat idea of the French mannered style

indicators.note: something offbeat is unconventional, so the word idea is set out in an unusual order

parts.note: de is the French word for of
camp is an affected, exaggerated, mannered style

explanation.surface: A personal assistant comes up with a quirky notion about an affected French fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'offbeat' is the anagram signal on 'idea'; 'gives' is a link. 'Personal assistant' is a loose but fair gloss for a senior officer's confidential aide.
explanation.definitionFit: An officer's confidential aide in the army serves as a general's personal helper.

clue.text: In his works we see man as he is and man as he 5 is not

definitions.text: In his works we see man as he is and man as he 5 is not

parts.words: In his works we see man as he is and man as he 5 is not
parts.note: plays on two novel titles by Robert ..., Man As He Is (1792) and Hermsprong, or Man As He Is Not (1796)

explanation.surface: A critic's claim that a writer shows humanity both truthfully and idealised.
explanation.definitionFit: The eighteenth-century novelist Robert Bage wrote both Man As He Is and Hermsprong, or Man As He Is Not, so both phrases are his titles.

clue.text: Valediction by T. H. White (on leaving London terminus?)

indicators.note: the station's name departs from White's title, so it is dropped from the end

parts.note: T. H. White wrote the novel Farewell Victoria (1933)
Victoria is a main railway terminus in London

explanation.surface: A goodbye from T. H. White, as if waving off a train from a London station.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaving' strips VICTORIA, a London rail terminus, from White's novel Farewell Victoria. 'on' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A valediction is a speech or word of parting, a goodbye.

clue.text: Terrible, evil, bad, crueller seducer

indicators.note: a terrible arrangement is a mess, so the letters of the three following words are jumbled

explanation.surface: A string of insults hurled at a cruel seducer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terrible' scrambles EVIL, BAD and CRUELLER, all fifteen letters, into the Hardy villain's name.
explanation.definitionFit: In Hardy's Tess of the d'Urbervilles this rich young man seduces Tess, so he is the novel's seducer.

clue.text: Noise in one kind of spirit

indicators.note: the noise word goes inside the word one, signalled by in

parts.note: a din is a loud noise

explanation.surface: A sound heard inside a single ghostly presence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Noise' looks like the subject of the surface but supplies the inserted piece; 'in' is the container signal. Ondine is also the title of Giraudoux's play about a water nymph.
explanation.definitionFit: An ondine, or undine, is a female water sprite of European folklore.

clue.text: Paladin, we hear, or a mere sergeant for Thackeray

indicators.note: says the paladin's name is to be taken as spoken, giving a word sounding the same but spelt otherwise

parts.note: Roland is the most famous of Charlemagne's paladins, hero of the Chanson de Roland

explanation.surface: A knight's name sounds like that of a humble soldier in a Thackeray story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we hear' turns the paladin Roland into a sound-alike spelling with a W, the name Thackeray gives a lowly sergeant.
explanation.definitionFit: Thackeray uses this name for a minor character of low rank, a sergeant, set against the noble paladin of legend.

clue.text: Prelate behind bush in meeting of bards

indicators.note: the prelate's letters come behind, after, the bush in the answer

parts.note: gorse is a spiny yellow-flowered bush
DD, Doctor of Divinity, is the degree held by senior clergy

explanation.surface: A bishop lurking behind a shrub at a gathering of poets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'behind' places the prelate's degree after the bush. A gorsedd is the Welsh assembly of bards held at the Eisteddfod.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gorsedd is the formal assembly of Welsh poets and druids, a gathering of bards.

clue.text: He came most carefully upon his hour

definitions.text: He came most carefully upon his hour

parts.words: He came most carefully upon his hour
parts.note: recasts Francisco's greeting in the opening scene of Hamlet, You come most carefully upon your hour, said to the arriving sentry

explanation.surface: A man is praised for arriving exactly on time.
explanation.definitionFit: In Hamlet's first scene the sentry relieving Francisco at midnight is greeted with these words for his punctuality.

clue.text: Provenance of a nineteenth-century nightingale

parts.note: the soprano Jenny Lind was billed as the Swedish Nightingale, so her homeland is meant, not a bird's

explanation.surface: Asking where a Victorian songbird came from.
explanation.definitionFit: Jenny Lind, the celebrated soprano nicknamed the Swedish Nightingale, was born in Stockholm.

clue.text: Virtuous chap, often seen with bird, however

parts.note: good means virtuous
a fellow is a chap

explanation.surface: A decent man often spotted with a feathered companion.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'bird' is Robin: Robin Goodfellow is Puck, the household sprite of English folklore. 'however' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The folklore sprite Puck is known as Robin Goodfellow, so the surname regularly follows a bird's name.

clue.text: Browning's was blunt on grey paper, in his scrofulous French novel

definitions.text: Browning's was blunt on grey paper, in his scrofulous French novel

parts.words: Browning's was blunt on grey paper, in his scrofulous French novel
parts.note: recalls Browning's Soliloquy of the Spanish Cloister, where the monk's scrofulous French novel is printed on grey paper with blunt lettering

explanation.surface: A description of the shabby printing of a racy book in a Browning poem.
explanation.definitionFit: Browning's lines read 'my scrofulous French novel / On grey paper with blunt' printing, the last word naming the lettering.

clue.text: "Oh you may laugh ac our dancing — It's all very well, it amuses you." (W. S. Gilbert)

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held is only a W. S. Gilbert quotation ('Oh you may laugh ac our dancing — It's all very well, it amuses you.') that neither contains nor points to SCHOOLERY; a word or gap is missing and searches did not find the full quotation.
annotationWithheld.clue: "Oh you may laugh ac our dancing — It's all very well, it amuses you." (W. S. Gilbert)

clue.text: Many herring to the crossing in Gaskell book

parts.note: a cran is a Scottish measure of fresh herring, so it stands for many of the fish
a ford is a shallow river crossing

explanation.surface: A shoal of fish heads for a river crossing in a Victorian novel.
explanation.walkthrough: A cran is a fishing measure of about 750 herring. 'to the' and 'in' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Elizabeth Gaskell's 1853 novel is set in a small town of genteel ladies and named after it.

clue.text: A very loud sort of a slut provides creative inspiration

parts.note: ff, fortissimo, is the musical marking for very loud

indicators.note: a sort of something is a version of it, so the letters of a slut are rearranged

explanation.surface: A coarse insult shouted at full volume somehow turns into a muse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' is the anagram signal on the second 'a' with 'slut'; the coarse surface hides a lofty word. 'provides' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Afflatus is a divine breath or impulse believed to inspire poets and artists.

clue.text: Mrs Perseus, and capital Russian, yes?

parts.note: Rome is the capital of Italy
da is the Russian for yes

explanation.surface: A question about the wife of a Greek hero and a Russian city.
explanation.walkthrough: Perseus rescued the princess chained to a rock and married her, hence 'Mrs Perseus'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Perseus saved the Ethiopian princess from a sea monster and made her his wife.

clue.text: Knot in Edith Wharton story

explanation.surface: A tangle in a tale by Edith Wharton.
explanation.definitionFit: A square knot used by sailors to shorten sail is so named, and Wharton's 1912 novel set in France bears the same title.

clue.text: Conradian murderee from The Silver Locket

indicators.note: says the name is taken out of the run of letters in the words that follow

explanation.surface: Identifying a murder victim in Conrad by a piece of jewellery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' points into 'silVER LOCket'. In Conrad's The Secret Agent, Mr Verloc is stabbed by his wife Winnie.
explanation.definitionFit: The secret agent of Conrad's novel is killed by his wife, so he is that book's murder victim.

clue.text: Novelist Francis is posh in the beginning

indicators.note: the posh letter is placed inside the word for beginning

parts.note: a start is a beginning
U is the label for upper-class, posh usage

explanation.surface: A claim that the novelist Francis was smart from the outset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts U, the old label for upper-class usage, inside START.
explanation.definitionFit: Francis Stuart was an Irish-Australian novelist, author of Black List, Section H.

clue.text: Simple direction for retiring actors

parts.note: retiring here means leaving the stage, and a script's direction for several players to depart is a single Latin word

explanation.surface: Sounds like advice for shy performers.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for 'they go out', it is the stage direction telling the players to leave.

clue.text: Celebratory Mendelssohn song

parts.note: points to Mendelssohn's Festgesang, known in English as his ... Song, a celebratory cantata

explanation.surface: A joyful piece by Mendelssohn.
explanation.definitionFit: Mendelssohn's Festgesang, written for the Gutenberg anniversary, is called his Festival Song, and the word also means celebratory.

clue.text: Strangely found in shotgun commonly used by Burns

indicators.note: signals that the word sits inside the letters of the next two words

explanation.surface: A shotgun used in a strange way, as a phrase from Robert Burns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'found in' points into 'shotgUN COmmonly'. 'used by Burns' says the definition is Scots, the dialect of the poet Robert Burns.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots the word means remarkably or strangely, as in the unco guid, the very righteous.

clue.text: William Styron did it in darkness: Ken Follett with lions

definitions.text: William Styron did it in darkness

explanation.surface: Two authors' characters resting, one in the dark and one among big cats.
explanation.definitionFit: Styron's first novel is Lie Down in Darkness and Follett's thriller is Lie Down with Lions, so both titles begin with the phrase.

clue.text: Circular tract?

parts.note: reads as a round plot of land, but a circular is a handbill and a tract a pamphlet

explanation.surface: Asks about a round stretch of land.
explanation.definitionFit: A small printed handbill or pamphlet handed out is both a circular and a tract.

clue.text: Strange, few discount loss of Wimsey case

indicators.note: strange means odd, so the letters of the next three words are put in an odd order

explanation.surface: A complaint that few will disregard a loss in a detective story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' scrambles FEW, DISCOUNT and LOSS into a Dorothy L. Sayers title; 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Clouds of Witness is the 1926 Dorothy L. Sayers novel in which Lord Peter Wimsey clears his brother of murder.
